allopack.title: The Water Cycle — Earth's Recycling System
allopack.author: AlloFlow flagship (authored by Claude, reviewed by A. Pomeranz)
allopack.standards: NGSS MS-ESS2-4 (water cycling through Earth systems driven by sunlight and gravity); CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.RST.6-8.4 (domain vocabulary)

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Water has been recycling itself on Earth for about four billion years — the water in your bottle once floated in a cloud, and maybe once sat in a glacier. Tonight you become a water-cycle expert.

1. Read **Journey of a Raindrop** first. Read it out loud if you can — or use the Read Aloud button.
2. Open the **Glossary** and play the **Crossword** and the **Word Scramble** until you win each one.
3. Keep **The Four Moves of Water** chart open while you work — it is your cheat sheet, and using it is allowed.
4. Try the **Sort It: Where Is the Water Going?** activity — drag each card to the right stage.
5. Take the **Check Your Understanding** quiz. It is not a grade — wrong answers just show us what to practice.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write two sentences about the water cycle in your own words.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Water Cycle** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Design Challenge: Where Should Our Rain Go?** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

When every goal below has a checkmark, you are done — and you have earned it. 🌧️➡️☀️

history.title: Journey of a Raindrop
history.data:
## Journey of a Raindrop

Right now, the Sun is lifting water into the sky — and it does not even touch it. Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, and puddles until some of the water changes from a liquid into an invisible gas called **water vapor**. This change is called **evaporation**. You have seen its results every time a puddle "disappears" on a sunny sidewalk. The puddle did not vanish. It moved.

Plants join in, too. Water travels up from the roots and escapes through tiny holes in the leaves — a process called **transpiration**. A single large tree can send hundreds of liters of water into the air on a hot day, like a slow, silent fountain.

High in the sky, the air is much colder. As water vapor cools, its molecules slow down and gather on tiny specks of dust and salt, changing back into liquid — billions of droplets so small they float. This is **condensation**, and a cloud is exactly that: a crowd of floating droplets, plus tiny ice crystals when the cloud is cold enough. A cloud is not made of smoke or cotton. It is water you can fly through.

Inside a cloud, droplets bump into each other and merge, growing heavier and heavier. When they grow too heavy for the rising air to keep them up, gravity wins. Water falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail — all of these are **precipitation**. Whether you get rain or snow depends mostly on how cold the air is on the way down.

Where does the fallen water go? Some of it flows downhill across the surface as **runoff**, joining streams and rivers that carry it back toward the ocean. Some soaks into the ground and becomes **groundwater**, filling the spaces between soil and rock like water filling a sponge. Lakes, rivers, oceans, and underground layers store the water in **collection** — until the Sun lifts it again.

Here is the amazing part: Earth almost never gets new water. The same water has been evaporating, condensing, falling, and collecting for about **four billion years**. The water in your water bottle may once have been in a dinosaur's pond, a Roman fountain, or a cloud over the ocean. The water cycle is Earth's original recycling system — powered by the Sun, pulled by gravity, and it never stops.

data.def: The change of liquid water into water vapor (a gas), usually caused by heat from the Sun.
The change of water vapor back into liquid droplets — this is how clouds form.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
Water gathering in oceans, lakes, rivers, and underground after it falls.
Water leaving a plant through tiny holes in its leaves and entering the air as vapor.
Water that flows over the land surface into streams and rivers instead of soaking in.
Water stored underground in the spaces between soil and rock.
Water in its gas form — invisible and mixed into the air.
The force that pulls precipitation down to Earth and pulls rivers toward the ocean.
A set of events that repeats in the same order, over and over, with no end.

data.title: Remember the Water Cycle
data.instructions: Each card locks in one set of facts from Journey of a Raindrop. Study the example aid, then build or personalize your own and explain how it points back to the real science.
data.sourceExcerpt: Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, and puddles until some of the water changes from a liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. This change is called evaporation. High in the sky, the air is much colder. As water vapor cools, its molecules slow down and gather on tiny specks of dust and salt, changing back into liquid. This is condensation. When droplets grow too heavy for the rising air to keep them up, gravity wins: precipitation. Lakes, rivers, oceans, and underground layers store the water in collection — until the Sun lifts it again.

cards.target: The four moves of water, in order: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection
essentialFacts: Evaporation: the Sun's energy turns liquid water into invisible water vapor.
Condensation: cooling vapor gathers on tiny specks and becomes liquid droplets — that is a cloud.
Precipitation: droplets or ice crystals grow heavy and fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
Collection: water gathers in oceans, lakes, rivers, ice, and underground until it evaporates again.
cards.aiExample: Every Cloud Pours Carefully. E-C-P-C: Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation, Collection.
cards.mapping: Each capital letter is the first letter of one move, and the sentence keeps them in the order water actually takes: it rises (E), gathers (C), falls (P), and rests (C) before the loop starts over.
scaffoldSteps: Write the four moves in order and circle their first letters: E, C, P, C.
Choose a word for each letter that also hints at the move (a word about clouds for C, about falling for P).
Read your sentence out loud and check that the order still matches rising, gathering, falling, resting.
coachPrompts: Which letter is repeated, and how will your sentence keep the two C words from swapping places?
Does your sentence hint at what each move does, or only at its letter?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own four-word sentence for E-C-P-C, or change the example so it sounds like you.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain how each word in your sentence leads back to one move of the water cycle.

hookFact.text: Earth almost never gets new water: the same water has cycled through these four moves for about four billion years.

cards.target: Water vapor is invisible; the white mist you can see is already liquid droplets
essentialFacts: Water vapor is a gas and cannot be seen.
Steam, fog, breath clouds, and cloud puffs are visible because they are tiny liquid droplets, not vapor.
Right above a kettle spout there is a short clear gap: that is where the real vapor is.
cards.aiExample: Picture a kettle. The empty-looking gap just above the spout is the invisible vapor. The white plume only begins where the air is cool enough for droplets to form. Clear gap = gas. White cloud = liquid.
cards.mapping: The picture puts the two ideas side by side in one place you have seen: the gap stands for vapor you cannot see, and the plume stands for droplets you can.
cards.scaffoldStarter: When I picture ____, the invisible part is ____ and the white part is ____.
scaffoldSteps: Choose a scene where mist appears: a kettle, your breath on a cold day, a hot shower.
Mark where the vapor is (invisible) and where the droplets are (white).
Say the rule the picture proves: if you can see it, it is already liquid.
coachPrompts: Where exactly in your picture is the vapor, and how do you know it is there if you cannot see it?
What cooled the vapor enough to make droplets in your scene?
cards.studentPrompt: Describe or sketch your own scene that separates invisible vapor from visible droplets.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture help you remember that vapor is invisible?

hookFact.text: The cloudy stuff above a boiling pot is not steam in the scientific sense; real water vapor is completely invisible.

cards.target: After rain, water takes two routes: runoff over the surface, or soaking in to become groundwater
essentialFacts: Runoff flows over the land surface into streams and rivers.
Groundwater soaks into the ground and fills the spaces between soil and rock.
Both routes end in collection: rivers carry water toward the ocean, and groundwater stores it underground.
cards.aiExample: A raindrop lands on a hill and meets a fork in the road. Its twin slides downhill over the grass, joins a stream, and rides all the way to the sea (runoff). It sinks between the soil grains instead, squeezes down past the roots, and settles into the gaps between rocks, where a well finds it years later (groundwater).
cards.mapping: The two twins keep the two routes apart in your memory: one stays on top and moves fast toward the ocean, one goes underneath and moves slowly into storage. Both are collection in the end.
cards.scaffoldStarter: A raindrop lands on ____. One twin ____ (runoff). The other twin ____ (groundwater).
scaffoldSteps: Pick a place the rain lands: a roof, a field, a hillside.
Send one twin over the surface and name where it ends up.
Send the other twin into the ground and name what it fills.
coachPrompts: What decides whether more water runs off or soaks in at your chosen spot?
Where does each twin finally rest, and why does that count as collection?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own two-twin story for a place you know.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does each twin's path match the definition of runoff or groundwater?

hookFact.text: Groundwater fills the spaces between soil and rock like water filling a sponge.

history.title: Sort It: Where Is the Water Going?

items.content: A puddle shrinks on a sunny sidewalk
A tree releases water through its leaves
Your cold drink glass gets wet on the outside
Tiny floating droplets crowd together in the sky
Hail bounces off a car roof
Rainwater soaks deep between soil and rock
A river carries water toward the ocean
Hot soup sends invisible water vapor into the air
Fog forms over a cold field in the morning

questions.question: A puddle disappears on a sunny day. What actually happened to the water?
options: It soaked down into the concrete and stayed there as liquid
The Sun's heat destroyed the water completely
It broke apart into oxygen and hydrogen gas
It changed into water vapor and mixed into the air
questions.correctAnswer: It changed into water vapor and mixed into the air

questions.question: What is a cloud made of?
options: Tiny floating water droplets and ice crystals
Smoke collected from the ground
Water vapor only, with no liquid or ice at all
Cotton-like fibers of frozen air
questions.correctAnswer: Tiny floating water droplets and ice crystals

questions.question: Why does condensation happen high in the sky?
options: The sky pushes water droplets together until they stick
Water vapor cools there and turns back into liquid
There is no gravity high in the sky
Clouds attract water from the ocean
questions.correctAnswer: Water vapor cools there and turns back into liquid

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a form of precipitation?
options: Snow falling on a mountain
Hail bouncing off a roof
Fog sitting over a field
Sleet hitting a window

questions.question: About how old is the water you drank today?
options: About four billion years — Earth keeps recycling the same water
Brand new, because rain creates fresh water each storm
Only a few hundred years old, recycled since colonial times
As old as the treatment plant that cleaned it
questions.correctAnswer: About four billion years — Earth keeps recycling the same water

questions.question: Explain the difference between runoff and groundwater. Where does each kind of water go?
questions.expectedAnswer: Runoff flows over the surface of the land into streams and rivers (and toward the ocean). Groundwater soaks into the ground and is stored in spaces between soil and rock.

questions.question: The water cycle is powered by two things: one lifts water up, one pulls it down. Name both and say what each one does.
questions.expectedAnswer: The Sun powers evaporation by warming water so it rises as vapor; gravity pulls precipitation down to Earth and pulls rivers toward the ocean.

history.title: But Wait — Water Questions Kids Actually Ask

data.question: Is it true I might be drinking dinosaur water? 🦕
data.answer: Pretty much! Earth has been recycling the same water for about four billion years, so the molecules in your bottle have been through countless clouds, rivers, and yes — probably a dinosaur or two.

data.question: Why doesn't the ocean overflow if rivers keep pouring into it?
data.answer: Because the Sun is constantly lifting water OUT of the ocean by evaporation — far more than rivers pour in. Most of that vapor falls right back on the ocean as rain, and the rest falls on land and returns through rivers and groundwater. Over a year, what leaves and what comes back balance out.

data.question: Why is rain fresh water when it evaporates from the salty ocean? 🧂
data.answer: Great catch — when water evaporates, the salt gets left behind. Only the water molecules rise as vapor, so clouds and rain are fresh water. (Rain can pick up tiny traces of salt from sea-spray specks in the air, but far too little to taste.)

data.question: Can the water cycle ever just stop?
data.answer: Not while the Sun shines and gravity pulls. It would take losing one of those to stop it — and neither is going anywhere for billions of years.

data.question: Where does my breath fog go on a cold day?
data.answer: That IS the water cycle, in miniature! Warm water vapor from your lungs hits cold air and condenses into tiny droplets — a little personal cloud — then evaporates again into the air.

data.question: Is snow just frozen rain?
data.answer: Not exactly. Snow forms when water vapor turns straight into ice crystals inside a very cold cloud. Sleet is closer to frozen rain — raindrops that freeze on the way down.

history.title: Design Challenge: Where Should Our Rain Go?
history.meta: 6th Grade • Design brief • proposal with labeled sketch

data.title: Where Should Our Rain Go?
data.instructions: Use what you learned about evaporation, runoff, groundwater, and collection to design a plan for the rain that lands on your school grounds. Frame the challenge, weigh options, build a proposal, test it against the facts, and revise.
data.fitReason: The lesson explains the two routes rain can take after it lands. A design brief asks students to steer that choice on purpose for a real place, which is where the runoff-versus-groundwater idea earns its keep.

brief.context: After a heavy rain, water pools on the paved play area, then streams across the parking lot into the street drain. The garden beds near the fence stay dry for days. The principal has asked a student team for ideas before the district repaves the lot next summer.
brief.audience: The principal and the facilities manager
brief.drivingQuestion: How should our school handle the rain that lands on the paved area so that more of it soaks in or gets stored instead of running straight into the street?
brief.seedDirection: Start from the two routes in the lesson: where on the grounds could runoff be slowed down, and where could water be given a chance to infiltrate?
lockedLessonFacts: After rain, some water flows over the surface as runoff and some soaks into the ground as groundwater.
Runoff moves downhill and gathers in streams, rivers, and drains; pavement gives it nowhere to soak in.
Groundwater fills the spaces between soil and rock and can be reached by plant roots and wells.
Water stored in soil, ponds, or tanks is part of collection, and the Sun eventually evaporates some of it again.
Gravity pulls water downhill, so the slope of a surface decides where runoff ends up.
openQuestions: How much of the paved area drains toward the street, and how much toward the beds?
What kind of soil is under the grass and beds, and how fast does it soak up water?
Are there rules about what can be built on school grounds or connected to the storm drain?
How much rain falls in a typical storm here?
stakeholders: Students who use the play area
Facilities staff who maintain the lot
Neighbors downhill from the street drain
criteria: Less water leaves the grounds as runoff after a typical storm
The play area still drains and is safe to use
The plan uses at least four glossary words correctly
Every claim about where water will go is tied to a lesson fact or marked as an assumption
constraints: No digging near buried utility lines
Must not send water toward the building foundation
Budget for a first version is small; the paving job is the main opportunity
Nothing that creates standing water for more than two days
brief.deliverable: A one-page proposal with a labeled sketch of the grounds showing where rain lands, where you want it to go, and one change that slows runoff or lets water soak in, plus a short explanation of the water-cycle reasoning behind it.

parallelExample.context: A town noticed its new shopping center flooded the road below it every storm.
parallelExample.move: Instead of a bigger drain, engineers cut the parking lot into sections that tilt toward planted strips, so runoff has to cross soil before it reaches the road. They measured how fast the soil soaked up water before deciding how wide the strips needed to be.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the same move you are making: change where gravity takes the water, and give it soil to infiltrate. It also shows that measuring the soil came before designing the fix.

supports.frameStarter: Right now rain that lands on ____ runs toward ____ because ____. We want more of it to ____.
frameChoices: Slow the runoff so it has time to soak in
Redirect the runoff toward soil or beds that need water
Store the water in a tank or pond for later use
Replace part of the pavement with a surface water can pass through
coachPrompts: Which of your claims about where the water goes could you check by watching the grounds during the next rain?
What happens to your design in a very heavy storm, or after a week of dry weather?
Which glossary word describes each arrow on your sketch?

data.coachHint: Trace the slope first. Everything else in the design follows from where gravity already sends the water.
data.sourceExcerpt: Some of it flows downhill across the surface as runoff, joining streams and rivers that carry it back toward the ocean. Some soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater, filling the spaces between soil and rock like water filling a sponge.
